'''Fátima de Madrid''' is the name given to an [[Arab]] [[Muslim]] [[astronomer]] and [[mathematician]] who supposedly lived during the late 10th and early 11th centuries in [[Al-Andalus|Islamic Spain]]. She was purportedly the daughter of the astronomer [[Maslama al-Majriti]], with whom she is said to have worked on several astronomical and mathematical treatises, including the astronomical tables of [[Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi]]. The earliest known account of her is the 1924 edition of the [[Enciclopedia universal ilustrada europeo-americana|Enciclopedia Espasa-Calpe]], and historians have cast doubt on whether she actually existed.<ref name=":0">{{cite book|last=Bernardi|first=Gabriella|contribution=Fátima of Madrid (Tenth Century)|doi=10.1007/978-3-319-26127-0_7|isbn=978-3-319-26127-0|location=Cham|pages=45–48|publisher=Springer|title=The Unforgotten Sisters: Female Astronomers and Scientists before Caroline Herschel|year=2016}}</ref>

== Purported career ==
Fátima de Madrid is said to have lived in [[Córdoba, Spain|Córdoba]], under the [[Caliphate of Córdoba]], during the late 10th and early 11th centuries. She is said to have been the daughter of the famous Islamic astronomer and scientist [[Maslama al-Majriti]].<ref name=":0" />

Her most famous supposed work, known as the "Corrections from Fátima," are a series of astronomical and mathematical treatises, though no copy of it has ever been found. She also supposedly co-authored "A Treatise on the Astrolabe" with her father, which contains information about how to use [[Astrolabe|astrolabes]]. Today, the manuscript is still allegedly preserved in the library of the monastery of [[El Escorial]].<ref name=":0" />

Fátima supposedly helped her father edit and adapt the astronomical tables of [[Muhammad ibn Musa al-Khwarizmi|al-Khwarizmi]], replacing the [[Solar Hijri calendar|Persian solar calendar]] used in his models with the [[Islamic calendar|Islamic lunar calendar]]. They supposedly corrected the tables also to account for the geographical location of Córdoba, as well as for the [[Meridian (geography)|meridian]] passing through it. With her father, she also supposedly translated the numeration of Persian to Arab years and determined the positions of the planets on the day of the [[Hegira|Hijra]]. Fátima also supposedly helped her father correct [[Ptolemy]]'s ''[[Almagest]]'', which contained mistakes in the calculations of eclipses.{{sfn|Núñez Valdés|2016}}

In addition, Fátima supposedly wrote several [[Zij|zījes]], a type of Islamic astronomical treatise. These covered topics including calendars, ephemerides of the planets, the Sun, and the Moon, and solar and lunar eclipses.{{sfn|Núñez Valdés|2016}}

Apart from her work on astronomy, Fátima was said to be able to speak, read, or write in [[Arabic]], [[Spanish language|Spanish]], [[Hebrew language|Hebrew]], [[Ancient Greek|Greek]], and [[Latin]].<ref name=":0" />

== Historicity ==
Whether Fátima de Madrid actually existed is contested. The earliest known reference to her existence is the 1924 edition of the [[Enciclopedia universal ilustrada europeo-americana|Enciclopedia Espasa-Calpe]]. As Ángel Requena Fraile, a [[History of mathematics|historian of mathematics]], explains:
{{Quote|text=In any project as ambitious as [the Enciclopedia Espasa-Calpe] there are errata, someone unscrupulous or some careless copyist. So a few myths are created, which are not documented, nor clothed by other sources, that refer to personages who should not be in the stories rather than myths. Francisco Vera, who is considered by many people as the father of the historiography of science in Spain, already warned when we he inquired about a  geometer, Bishop of Calahorra in the Visigoth era,  called Luciniano, that appears only in the Espasa and in no other sources. We have this situation with Fátima, the clever daughter of Maslama. We find something similar to what happens with Luciniano. There is no reference, no original or reliable source on which to stand.<ref>{{cite web|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20130717223753/https://www.andalucia.cc/viva/mujer/vidas/fatima_de_madrid.html|archive-date=2013-07-17|url=https://www.andalucia.cc/viva/mujer/vidas/fatima_de_madrid.html|url-status=dead|title=Fátima de Madrid ¿Astrónoma? S. X-XI|language=es|first=Ángel|last=Requena Fraile}} As translated by {{cite report|title=Did Fátima de Madrid really exist?|last=Núñez Valdés|first=Juan|year=2016|hdl=11441/62073}}</ref>}}Arabist, historian, and biographer of [[Al-Andalus]] Manuela Marín similarly holds that Fátima is a historical invention from the Espasa-Calpe. Marín attributes continued discussion about her, such as on the internet and with her inclusion in a 2009 calendar titled "Astronomers who made history", to uncritical repetition of the Espasa-Calpe's content.<ref>{{Cite encyclopedia|last=Marín|quote=Se trata, por tanto, del más ilustre de los madrileños andalusíes, y no hacía falta que se le inventase, como así ha sido, una históricamente inexistente hija suya, a la que se ha llamado «Fátima de Madrid» y que asombrosamente ha sido incluida en el calendario “Astrónomas que hicieron historia”, editado con motivo del Año Internacional de la astronomía (2009). El error, que procede de una vieja edición de la Enciclopedia Espasa, se ha ido reproduciendo acríticamente, ya va siendo hora que se deshaga, aunque su abundante circulación en Internet no da muchas esperanzas en ese sentido.|oclc=798943110|pages=191|location=Madrid|isbn=978-84-9785-707-9|year=2011|publisher=Casa Árabe|first=Manuela|editor-first2=María Dolores|editor-last2=Algora Weber|title=De Mayrit a Madrid: Madrid y los árabes, del siglo IX al siglo XXI|editor1-first=Daniel|editor1-last=Gil Flores|entry=Arabismo en Madrid}}</ref>
